official_kr_name: Rice blast (LPDK); leaf blast and panicle blast listed separately in NCPMS
f1_names: NCPMS lists leaf blast and panicle blast separately under paddy rice. LPDK lists rice blast, with ear blight as a second name, and gives *Pyricularia oryzae* Cavara (sexual morph *Magnaporthe oryzae* B.C. Couch). It also retains a separate *P. grisea* / *M. grisea* row under the same disease name. NCPMS uses the older name *Magnaporthe grisea* and associates it with the asexual morph *Pyricularia oryzae*. EPPO's preferred name is *Pyricularia oryzae* Cavara (PYRIOR); synonyms include *Dactylaria oryzae* and *Magnaporthe oryzae*. English names include rice blast, rotten neck of rice, and seedling blight of rice. IRRI has separate fact sheets for leaf/collar blast and node/neck blast. The original research could not access the APS page (HTTP 403); the English name rice blast has now been cross-checked separately during the naming review. [Source 1](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00004234&totalSearchYn=Y) [Source 2](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000815&totalSearchYn=Y) [Source 3](https://genebank.rda.go.kr/english/plntDissInfoMain.do) [Source 4](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/PYRIOR) [Source 5](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/blast-leaf-collar)
f2_parts_stages: Affects above-ground tissues including leaves, collars, nodes, panicle necks, and panicles at all growth stages. Adult-plant resistance reduces leaf blast; infection can kill plants from the seedling to tillering stages (IRRI). In Korea, seed transmission can produce nursery lesions; main-field disease occurs mainly from late June. Panicle infection occurs around heading, with upper-leaf lesions as major inoculum sources. Neck infection before the milk stage prevents grain formation (NCPMS; IRRI). [Source 1](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/blast-leaf-collar) [Source 2](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00004234&totalSearchYn=Y) [Source 3](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/blast-node-neck)
f3_symptoms: The leaves have white to gray-green initial lesions with dark green borders, and as they age, they become spindle-shaped, diamond-shaped lesions with a gray-white center and red-brown edges ([IRRI RKB leaf · leaf collar](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/blast-leaf-collar), How to identify). NCPMS writes that the chronic type has red edges, the acute type is covered with gray mold (conidium), and in severe cases, the entire plant becomes red and cannot grow (stunting) ([NCPMS leaf blast](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00004234&totalSearchYn=Y), symptom description). A band-shaped black to gray-brown lesion develops at the node and becomes bent, and the panicle neck is surrounded by a gray-brown lesion and the ear becomes an unfilled grain ([IRRI RKB node·panicle neck](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/blast-node-neck); [NCPMS panicle blast](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000815&totalSearchYn=Y), symptom description)).
f4_confusions: In the brown spot, the lesion is more rounded, brown, and has a yellow halo ([IRRI RKB leaf·leaf collar](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/blast-leaf-collar), comparison paragraph at the bottom). Like rice blast, brown spots do not invade quickly from the tip of the ear or create whiteheads ([NCPMS brown spot](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000750&totalSearchYn=Y), end of symptom description). The whitehead of panicle neck·node blast is similar to the damage of striped rice stem borer ([IRRI RKB node·panicle neck](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/blast-node-neck)).) In LPDK, there is a separate 'false blast' (*Alternaria oryzae*, *Cladosporium herbarum*) with a similar name ([LPDK](https://genebank.rda.go.kr/english/plntDissInfoMain.do), false blast line). An authoritative source for direct comparison with cold injury, herbicide phytotoxicity, and potassium deficiency is unverified.
f5_differentiation:
*Features assessable in photographs:* Spindle-shaped·lozenge-shaped lesion, gray-white center and red-brown border, early dark green border, band-shaped dark-brown lesion at the node, gray-brown lesion surrounding the panicle neck, gray mold on the surface of the acute lesion ([IRRI RKB leaf·leaf collar](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/blast-leaf-collar); [NCPMS leaf blast](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00004234&totalSearchYn=Y), symptom description)). Depending on the variety, lesions may overlap with brown spot (IRRI two pages specify mutual confusion).
*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* If the whitehead stem comes out by pulling it, it is a striped rice stem borer. If it does not fall out, it is a panicle neck·node blast ([IRRI RKB node·panicle neck](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/blast-node-neck), How to identify bullet point). Ask about nitrogen and livestock manure compost application amount, cold water inflow, and heading stage rainfall ([NCPMS leaf blast](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00004234&totalSearchYn=Y), occurrence environment/control method).
*Features requiring laboratory tests:* The conidium is a colorless pyriform, 2 septum, 14~37 × 5~12 µm, and produces a dark brown perithecium in the medium ([NCPMS leaf blast](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00004234&totalSearchYn=Y), pathogen characteristics). Since it is clearly different from the cylindrical 6-14 septum spores of brown spot fungus, the two diseases can be clearly distinguished through microscopic examination. Official PCR·ELISA protocols and moist-chamber incubation standard procedures are unverified.
f6_conditions: NCPMS gives fungal growth at 8–37 °C, optimum 25–28 °C, and conidium production at 12–34 °C, without identifying the original experiments. Frequent rain, cool summers including cold injury, humid weather around heading, and excessive nitrogen favor outbreaks. IRRI lists low soil moisture, frequent prolonged showers, cool daytime temperatures, and dew associated with large day–night temperature differences. Silicate application can reduce disease in silicon-deficient soil. Infection thresholds for leaf-wetness duration and relative humidity were not verified. [Source 1](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00004234&totalSearchYn=Y) [Source 2](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/blast-leaf-collar)

f1_names: NCPMS lists it as **sheath blight** (紋枯病, Sheath blight) and writes the pathogen as *Thanatephorus cucumeris* (Frank) Donk ([NCPMS sheath blight](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000813&totalSearchYn=Y), basic information·pathogen information). LPDK identifies the current pathogen as *Rhizoctonia solani* J.G. Kühn, write the sexual morph as *T. cucumeris* and the synonym as *Moniliopsis solani* and *Pellicularia solani* ([LPDK](https://genebank.rda.go.kr/english/plntDissInfoMain.do), sheath blight line). The EPPO preferred name is *R. solani* Kühn (RHIZSO), and synonyms include *Corticium solani*, *Pellicularia filamentosa*, and *Hypochnus solani*, and "sheath blight of rice" was not confirmed in the common name list (list was truncated) ([EPPO RHIZSO](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/RHIZSO), Overview). **The anastomosis group AG1-IA notation is nowhere in LPDK, NCPMS, or IRRI** ([IRRI RKB sheath blight](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/sheath-blight), What it does).
f2_parts_stages: Symptoms usually appear in the tillering stage~milk stage, and in flooded rice fields, it starts from the leaf sheath just above the water surface and spreads to the upper leaf sheath, leaves, and neighboring plants ([IRRI RKB sheath blight](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/sheath-blight), How to identify·What it does). In Korea, sclerotium is mostly formed in **late July to early August** and the lesion gradually moves upward ([NCPMS sheath blight](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000813&totalSearchYn=Y), symptom description).
f3_symptoms: Oval-shaped gray-green lesions of 1 to 3 cm in length appear on the leaf sheath, and as they age, the center becomes gray-white and the edges turn brown ([IRRI RKB sheath blight](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/sheath-blight), How to identify). In NCPMS, water-soaked oval lesions that look like they have been blanched grow dark green and the surrounding area turns light brown, and sclerotium is usually written as a 1-2 mm brown circle** ([NCPMS sheath blight](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000813&totalSearchYn=Y), symptom description and pathogen characteristics).
f4_confusions: IRRI identifies stem rot and stem-borer injury as possible confusions and recommends examining leaf-sheath lesions and sclerotia. LPDK lists several related rice diseases separately: sheath eyespot (*R. cerealis*), sheath spot (*R. oryzae*), aggregate sheath spot (*R. oryzae-sativae*), other sclerotial diseases including a gray sclerotial disease, stem rot (*Magnaporthe salvinii*), sheath rot (*Sarocladium*, *Pantoea ananatis*), and sheath brown rot (*Pseudomonas fuscovaginae*). The original research did not verify sources describing symptom differences among these diseases or comparisons with abiotic disorders. English descriptions of the less familiar Korean sclerotial-disease labels here are descriptive, rather than verified standardized common names. [Source 1](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/sheath-blight) [Source 2](https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/key-server/data/0e090d01-0209-460e-810c-0d060708030c/media/Html/Sheath_blight.htm) [Source 3](https://genebank.rda.go.kr/english/plntDissInfoMain.do)
f5_differentiation:
*Features assessable in photographs:* A 1-3 cm grey-green oval lesion starting from the leaf sheath near the water surface or ground, with a grey-white center and brown border, and a 1-2 mm brown sclerotium ([IRRI RKB sheath blight](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/sheath-blight); [NCPMS sheath blight](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000813&totalSearchYn=Y), pathogen characteristics). However, since it overlaps with other *Rhizoctonia* type sclerotium diseases, it is treated as 'suspicious'.
*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* Close-up photo of sclerotium, nitrogen fertilization amount, dense planting, and variety ([NCPMS sheath blight](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000813&totalSearchYn=Y), occurrence environment).
*Features requiring laboratory tests:* The pathogen spreads through mycelium and does not produce airborne spores (IRRI). Authoritative procedures for anastomosis-group determination by hyphal anastomosis or ITS analysis, and for distinguishing similar *Rhizoctonia* species, were not verified. A Korean study reporting AG-1 in 1,091 of 2,276 isolates, including 791 IA isolates, was available only as a search snippet; the full text was not verified. [Source 1](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/sheath-blight) [Source 2](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000813&totalSearchYn=Y)
f6_conditions: Domestic standards: Temperature for invasion **22~35 ℃, optimal 30~32 ℃**, frequent occurrence when **humidity above 96%** persists between planting, excessive nitrogen, dense planting, cultivation period, and variety are affected (no original paper notation) ([NCPMS sheath blight](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000813&totalSearchYn=Y), occurrence environment). IRRI standards: 28-32 ℃, high nitrogen, canopy RH 85-100%, rainy season, dense planting, floating sclerotium, high-yield varieties; The diseased crop produces up to 2 million sclerotium per m² ([IRRI RKB sheath blight](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/sheath-blight), Why and where it occurs). Rice Doctor attributed the source of sclerotium levels to Chien et al. Write 1969 ([Rice Doctor Sheath blight](https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/key-server/data/0e090d01-0209-460e-810c-0d060708030c/media/Html/Sheath_blight.htm)). IRRI writes that there are no resistant varieties for cultivation.

f1_names: NCPMS lists it as **brown spot** (胡麻葉枯病), and the English name has a typo as "Heliminthosporium blight, Helminthosporium leaf". The pathogen is *Cochliobolus miyabeanus* (Ito & Kuribayashi) Drechsler ex Dastur, asexual morph and is listed as *Helminthosporium oryzae*, *Drechslera oryzae*, and *Bipolaris oryzae* ([NCPMS brown spot](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000750&totalSearchYn=Y), basic information/pathogen information). LPDK carries the current name *Bipolaris oryzae* (Breda de Haan) Shoemaker, synonym *C. miyabeanus*, English name Helminthosporium blight/leaf spot, Brown spot·Ear blight, and the second national name 'Ear blight' ([LPDK](https://genebank.rda.go.kr/english/plntDissInfoMain.do), brown spot line). The EPPO preferred name is *B. oryzae*(COCHMI), *Ophiobolus miyabeanus* is added to the synonym, and the English name is brown spot of rice, etc. ([EPPO COCHMI](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/COCHMI), Overview).
f2_parts_stages: Infects coleoptiles, leaves, leaf sheaths, panicle branches, glumes, and spikelets. Disease occurs at all stages, with infection from maximum tillering to grain filling particularly important (IRRI). NCPMS reports a rapid increase after panicle initiation and greater susceptibility of lower leaves; panicle infection affecting yield occurs up to 25 days after heading. [Source 1](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/brown-spot) [Source 2](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000750&totalSearchYn=Y)
f3_symptoms: Small, round, dark-brown to purplish leaf spots enlarge into circular or oval lesions with light-brown to gray centers and reddish-brown margins. Lesions are 5–14 mm in susceptible varieties and pinhead-sized in resistant varieties. Dark-brown to black oval spots occur on glumes and panicle branches; grains develop pecky rice (IRRI). NCPMS describes a yellow toxic halo around the initial dark-brown necrotic area, later concentric rings, and dark-brown streaks on panicle stalks. [Source 1](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/brown-spot) [Source 2](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000750&totalSearchYn=Y)
f4_confusions: In some varieties, it can be mistaken for rice blast ([IRRI RKB brown spot](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/brown-spot), last paragraph). It is closely related to abiotic factors: It is common in soils with water stress, nutrient deficiency, and accumulation of toxic substances ([IRRI RKB brown spot](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/brown-spot), Why and where it occurs), and is also common in Korea in old rice fields, peat soils, sandy soils, and shallow hard soils ([NCPMS brown spot](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000750&totalSearchYn=Y), occurrence environment). Zinc deficiency is described as similar to iron deficiency/iron toxicity, producing "dusty brown spots" in the upper leaves and brown blotches/streaks in the lower leaves, but this page does not directly compare brown spots (indirect evidence) ([Rice Doctor Zinc deficiency](https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/key-server/data/0e090d01-0209-460e-810c-0d060708030c/media/Html/Zinc_deficiency.htm)).

f1_names: NCPMS lists it as **bacterial blight**(白葉枯病, Bacterial blight), but in the pathogen name column, the old name *X. campestris* pv. *oryzae* (Ishiyama) Dye, and in the text 'pathogen characteristics' on the same page, *X. oryzae* pv. The notation is mixed by writing *oryzae* ([NCPMS bacterial blight](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000744&totalSearchYn=Y), pathogen information). LPDK's current name for bacterial blight (Bacterial leaf blight) is *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzae* (Ishiyama) Swings et al., synonym *X. campestris* pv. Write *oryzae* ([LPDK](https://genebank.rda.go.kr/english/plntDissInfoMain.do), bacterial blight line). EPPO(XANTOR) synonym is *Bacillus/Bacterium/Phytomonas/Pseudomonas oryzae*, *X. campestris* pv. *oryzae*, *Xanthomonas kresek*, and its English name is bacterial blight of rice, bacterial leaf blight (BLB), kresek disease ([EPPO XANTOR](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTOR), Overview).
f2_parts_stages: Causes seedling wilt (kresek) and leaf yellowing and drying. Infection at booting affects grain quality and the proportion of broken rice more than yield (IRRI). In Korea it usually appears around heading, but in regularly affected fields it can occur early in the main field and occasionally in nurseries. Sudden wilting and death can occur from 20–30 days after transplanting through peak tillering. Symptoms mainly affect leaf blades and sheaths, and occasionally grains (NCPMS). [Source 1](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bacterial-blight) [Source 2](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000744&totalSearchYn=Y)
f3_symptoms: Water-soaked to yellowish-orange stripes appear at the tip, edge, and wound of the leaf, and the **edge is wavy** as it progresses toward the base of the leaf. On young lesions, milky bacterial ooze forms early in the morning, and when it dries, it turns into yellow beads. Old lesions become yellow to grayish white and black dots appear due to saprophytic microorganisms ([IRRI RKB bacterial blight](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bacterial-blight), How to identify). NCPMS states that infiltrative lesions on the edge 5 to 6 cm below the tip of the leaf blade spread up and down to yellow/orange yellow and fade to white to grayish white after 2 to 3 days ([NCPMS bacterial blight](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000744&totalSearchYn=Y), symptom description).
f4_confusions: Kresek can be confused with early striped rice stem-borer injury (IRRI). Leaf symptoms closely resemble bacterial leaf streak caused by Xoc and become difficult to distinguish as disease progresses (EPPO). Details of the diagnostic differences are discussed in the differentiation field; photograph-based identification alone does not establish the pathovar. [Source 1](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bacterial-blight) [Source 2](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTOR/datasheet) [Source 3](https://genebank.rda.go.kr/english/plntDissInfoMain.do)
f5_differentiation:
*Features assessable in photographs:* Yellow-orange to yellow-white lesions with wavy borders starting from the leaf tips and edges, milky ooze drops on young lesions in the early morning, and dry yellow beads ([IRRI RKB bacterial blight](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bacterial-blight)). Contrast with the straight edges of Xoc ([EPPO XANTTO datasheet](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTTO/datasheet), Symptoms))
*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* Squeeze the bottom of the kresek seedling to check for yellow ooze, making sure it is not easily pulled out; Cut a young lesion, place it in clear water, and after a few minutes, see if a cloudy liquid flows from the cut surface ([IRRI RKB bacterial blight](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bacterial-blight), How to identify). Recent flooding status and time, typhoon, nitrogen fertilization amount ([NCPMS bacterial blight](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000744&totalSearchYn=Y), occurrence environment).
*Features requiring laboratory tests:* Gram-negative rods (1~2 × 0.8 µm, one polar flagellum), Yellow round colonies appear on nutrient medium for 3-4 days. Optimal 26~30 ℃ ([NCPMS bacterial blight](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000744&totalSearchYn=Y), pathogen characteristics). PSA·NBY·GF·semi-selective medium separation, seedling test, bacteriophage, IF, ELISA, (real-time) PCR, seed bio-PCR, **Xoo/Xoc discrimination TaqMan multiplex PCR·LAMP**, race-specific PCR for domestic K3a race (Song et al. 2012, 2014) and detailed procedures are in EPPO PM 7/80 ([EPPO XANTOR datasheet](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTOR/datasheet), Detection and identification).
f6_conditions: IRRI and EPPO list 25–34 °C and RH above 70%; strong winds and prolonged heavy rain disperse bacterial ooze, and excessive nitrogen increases severity. EPPO cites Mew et al. 1993 and identifies floodwater and irrigation as major routes. NCPMS reports high occurrence at July mean temperatures of 22–24 °C, major outbreaks with July rainfall at least 200 mm and winds at least 15 m/s, and disease incidence of 8.8% after 12-hour flooding versus 72.7% after 48-hour flooding. Rainfall from late July to late August is important. Host weeds include *Leersia* grasses; bacteriophage density can provide a warning 10–15 days in advance. The original experiments are not identified. The original report recommends prioritizing Korean values in Korean risk models, with IRRI/EPPO ranges alongside them. [Source 1](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bacterial-blight) [Source 2](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTOR/datasheet) [Source 3](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000744&totalSearchYn=Y)
f7_occurrence: Korea: The first literature on LPDK is Mu Nae-kyo, Joseon Dynasty Prefectural Government 5:62 (**1930**) and Lee Gyeong-hwi et al. 1965 ([LPDK](https://genebank.rda.go.kr/english/plntDissInfoMain.do), bacterial blight line). The EPPO datasheet, citing a Korean paper, shows that the domestic occurrence area increased more than 10 times between 2002 and 2005, reaching approximately 27,000 ha (Noh et al. 2007), who wrote that the 2003 outbreak caused large losses with the emergence of a new race **K3a** (Jeung et al. 2006; Original paper not read, re-cited) ([EPPO XANTOR datasheet](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTOR/datasheet), Impact). Overseas: EPPO lists South Korea and North Korea as “Present, restricted distribution,” and Asian distribution countries include Bangladesh, China, India, Indonesia, Japan (Honshu and Kyushu), the Philippines, and Vietnam. There are no known outbreaks in the EPPO region ([EPPO XANTOR distribution](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTOR/distribution)).

There is only *oryzicola* ([KR-Notice Annex 2](https://www.law.go.kr/LSW/flDownload.do?flSeq=169519059)). Bacteria, item 9) and is not a priority pest ([EU-2072](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:02019R2072-20261015); [EU-1702](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_del/2019/1702/oj)). United States: **PPQ select agent**(7 CFR 331.3(b)(6) "Xanthomonas oryzae", species-specific pv. *oryzae* included), listed as APHIS Pests of Concern ([US-331](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-7/section-331.3); [US-PoC](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/laws-regs/animal-plant-diseases-pests-concern)). China: **检疫性有害生物** "水稻白叶枯病菌"([CN](https://assets.ippc.int/static/media/files/reportingobligation/2025/01/07/CATALOGUE_OF_QUARANTINE_PESTS_FOR_IMPORT_PLANTS_TO_THE_PEOPLES_REPUBLIC_OF_CHINA_updated_20241128.doc)). Japan: not listed(verified)([JP](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/325M50010000073)). Australia: unverified. Since it is a domestically endemic disease, its absence from the Korean list does not contradict the legal definition (undistributed pests domestically), but the overseas regulatory status should not be transferred to the Korean status.

f1_names: **Official Korean disease name: unverified (no registration).** In LPDK, 9 bacterial diseases of the host rice and all genus names *Xanthomonas* were searched, but *oryzicola* records were 0 ([LPDK Search](https://genebank.rda.go.kr/plntDissInfoMain.do),Host rice bacteria result table·*Xanthomonas* result table), there is no Xoc item in the NCPMS disease name search ([NCPMS disease list](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoListRM.np),Korean name/English name search). **Note: “rice bacterial streak disease” (DSNM_NO 869) in LPDK is *Acidovorax avenae* subsp. It is a disease** of *avenae* (Hoo-seop Jeong et al. 1980), and EPPO calls this *Acidovorax* disease “bacterial brown stripe of rice” ([LPDK search](https://genebank.rda.go.kr/plntDissInfoMain.do); [EPPO XANTTO datasheet](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTTO/datasheet), Detection paragraph)). In the domestic quarantine review, non-occurring bacterial diseases in Korea are unified by English name and written only as “Bacterial leaf streak” ([Hong Yeon-seok et al. 2020](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO202029462559364.pdf), Introduction last paragraph·Table 1 No. 38). EPPO preferred name is *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzicola* (Fang et al.) Swings et al. (XANTTO) and the synonym is *X. campestris* pv. *oryzicola*, *X. oryzicola*, *X. translucens* f. sp. *oryzicola*, English name is bacterial leaf streak (BLS) ([EPPO XANTTO](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTTO), Overview). It was first observed in the Philippines in 1918, but was long mistaken for bacterial blight, and was named *X. oryzicola* in China in 1957, and reclassified as pathovar in 1990 ([EPPO XANTTO datasheet](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTTO/datasheet), Notes on taxonomy).
f2_parts_stages: Primarily affects leaf blades; infected florets become brown or black, and infected seeds show glume browning and endosperm necrosis (EPPO). Effects are important from maximum tillering to panicle initiation, while mature rice recovers more readily (IRRI). Both pathovars have been isolated from the seed coat, but the cited EPPO account reports seed transmission for Xoc only. Xoc can survive for up to 5 months in seed stored at 15–30 °C. [Source 1](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTTO/datasheet) [Source 2](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bacterial-leaf-streak)
f3_symptoms: Narrow, dark green water-soaked stripes between leaf veins with a yellow border turn yellow-orange to brown and merge, forming small amber-colored bacterial ooze droplets, which dry out to brown to gray at the end ([EPPO XANTTO datasheet](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTTO/datasheet), Symptoms). The lesion is **translucent** when held up to light ([IRRI RKB BLS](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bacterial-leaf-streak), How to identify). It is often accompanied by moth larvae and rice leaf beetle stains ([EPPO XANTTO datasheet](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTTO/datasheet), Symptoms).
f4_confusions: Advanced Xoc leaf streak and Xoo bacterial blight may be difficult to distinguish and may occur on the same leaf. Xoc lesions have straight edges; bacterial-blight lesions have wavy edges. Xoc enters through stomata or wounds and colonizes intercellular spaces in the mesophyll; Xoo enters through hydathodes and colonizes vascular tissue (EPPO). Biochemical, pathogenicity, or serological testing may be needed (IRRI). Narrow brown spot, associated in LPDK with *Cercospora oryzae*, is not translucent and does not produce bacterial ooze. A source comparing abiotic disorders was not verified. [Source 1](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTTO/datasheet) [Source 2](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bacterial-leaf-streak) [Source 3](https://genebank.rda.go.kr/plntDissInfoMain.do)
f5_differentiation:
*Features assessable in photographs:* narrow water-soaked stripes between leaf veins; Straight lesion edges, backlight translucent, amber bacterial ooze droplets, With pest marks ([EPPO XANTTO datasheet](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTTO/datasheet); [IRRI RKB BLS](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bacterial-leaf-streak)).) Definitive differentiation from bacterial blight and determination of pathovar is impossible with photographs.
*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* A field test showing that if you cut off the advanced part of the lesion and put it in a cup of water, the water becomes cloudy after 5 minutes ([IRRI RKB BLS](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bacterial-leaf-streak)).) Whether or not imported seeds and breeding materials were used (the main route for long-distance spread is seeds), recent rainfall, strong winds, and high temperatures, and the amount of nitrogen fertilization ([EPPO XANTTO datasheet](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTTO/datasheet), Pathways·Biology).
*Features requiring laboratory tests:* PSA·NBY·GF·semi-selective medium separation (XOS medium for seeds; saprophytic *Pantoea* can cover slow-growing Xoc), detached leaf inoculation method, IF·ELISA (commercial kit), Xoc-specific PCR (Kang et al. 2008), Xoc/Xoo distinction TaqMan multiplex, LAMP, Xoc·Xoo·*B. glumae*Simultaneous detection multiplex PCR, biochemical discrimination (Xoc is acetoin production, L-alanine sole carbon source growth, 0.2% casamino acids growth positive, Cu(NO₃)₂ 0.001% resistance negative), pathogenicity test for 30-45 day old seedlings of susceptible varieties ([EPPOhttps://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTTO/datasheet), Detection and identification methods). There is an EPPO diagnostic standard PM 7/80 (only confirms existence) ([EPPO XANTTO documents](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTTO/documents)).Domestic literature summarizes the detection of TXT/TXT4R primers after plating on GF medium (yellow colonies) or mXOS medium (red colonies) ([Hong Yeon-seok et al. 2020](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO202029462559364.pdf),(around p.140). Since this is an unrecorded and regulated quarantine pest in Korea, suspected samples need to be confirmed by a quarantine agency.
f6_conditions: Post-infection temperature is the main determining factor, with progression occurring at 26-32 ℃ and suppression below 22 ℃ (as cited in Devadath 1984). Secondary infections do not occur without sustained rainfall, and only very wet conditions cause damage, and large amounts of nitrogen encourage outbreaks. In water, it survives up to 90 days at 15-20 ℃ and up to 60 days at 25-45 ℃ ([EPPO XANTTO datasheet](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTTO/datasheet), Biology paragraphs 5-7). Yield loss is 8-17% in the rainy season, 1-3% in the dry season (IRRI), 5-30% in central India, 10-20% in southern China (up to 40%), and up to 60% in Uganda ([IRRI RKB BLS](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bacterial-leaf-streak), Why is it important; [EPPO XANTTO datasheet](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTTO/datasheet), Economic impact).

f1_names: NCPMS lists **bakanae disease**(馬塵苗病, Bakanae disease) and writes the pathogen as *Fusarium moniliforme*, *Gibberella fujikuroi* (Sawada) **Ito** [asexual morph *F. fujikuroi*] ([NCPMS bakanae disease](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000752), basic information·pathogen information). LPDK lists *Fusarium fujikuroi* Nirenberg as the pathogen and *G. fujikuroi* (Sawada) **Wollenw.** as the synonym ([LPDK search](https://genebank.rda.go.kr/plntDissInfoMain.do), host rice result table). EPPO preferred name is *F. fujikuroi* Nirenberg (GIBBFU), synonym is *G. fujikuroi* (Sawada) Wollenweber, *Lisea fujikuroi* ([EPPO GIBBFU](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/GIBBFU), Overview). The synonym name notation is different in NCPMS (Ito) and LPDK·EPPO (Wollenw.). In a study on rice seeds in 10 Asian countries, *F. fujikuroi* was dominant, *F. fujikuroi*·*F. concentricum* caused typical bakanae elongation symptoms, and *F. proliferatum*·*F. verticillioides* only caused shrinkage (confirmed through search summary, main text Unviewed)([PMC3905127](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3905127)).) There is also a report that many of the old "*F. proliferatum*" notations were changed to *F. annulatum*, etc. in the re-identification of domestic FFSC preserved strains ([JBNU](https://pure.jbnu.ac.kr/en/publications/the-fusarium-fujikuroi-species-complex-in-korea-taxonomic-revisio/)).) (search summary)([JBNU](https://pure.jbnu.ac.kr/en/publications/the-fusarium-fujikuroi-species-complex-in-korea-taxonomic-revisio/)).)
f2_parts_stages: Disease begins with seed transmission and appears in nurseries from about 10 days after sowing, during main-field tillering, after maximum tillering, at booting, and at heading. Spores enter rice flowers at flowering and persist latently in seed (NCPMS). Root and crown infection leads to systemic fungal growth (IRRI). [Source 1](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000752) [Source 2](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bakanae)
f3_symptoms: In the nursery, affected seedlings may grow to at least 1.5 times normal height, then become stunted and die within 1–2 weeks; heavily infected seedlings can die without elongation. In the main field, white mycelium and spores appear on leaf sheaths after 2–3 weeks, with light-brown nodes, aerial roots at upper nodes, poor heading, and sterility (NCPMS). IRRI describes slender yellow-green plants, reduced tillering, white powdery fungal growth at the stem base, and roots on above-ground nodes; infected plants can also be stunted or appear normal. Of 15 Korean field isolates of *F. fujikuroi*, 9 caused stunting and 6 caused typical elongating bakanae symptoms; stunting isolates produced no gibberellin or 10–15 times less (Niehaus et al. 2017). [Source 1](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000752) [Source 2](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bakanae) [Source 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5675463/)
f4_confusions: Distinction from regular stamped seedlings (high temperature, overcrowding, and excessive nitrogen): In bakanae disease seedlings, the 1st and 2nd true leaves are separated by more than 45° or the 2nd and 3rd true leaves do not emerge, and when pulled, the stem and seeds are easily separated (painted seedlings are pulled out together). If it is determined based solely on outgrowth, the actual latent infection rate can be more than 10 times higher ([NCPMS bakanae disease](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000752), symptom description). Official comparative data on nitrogen overgrowth itself is unverified.
f5_differentiation:
*Features assessable in photographs:* Height difference within the seedbed (more than 1.5 times), light green/yellow-green leaf color, 1st and 2nd true leaves angle 45° or more, 2nd and 3rd true leaves not appearing, white mycelium/spores at the base of the stem, aerial rooting of above-ground nodes, browning of nodes ([NCPMS bakanae disease](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000752); [IRRI RKB Bakanae](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bakanae)).) Take a picture of the entire seedbed rather than a single individual. It is necessary. **You should not test negative just because you do not have bakanae elongation symptoms** (majority of stunting type).
*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* Pull up individual seedlings and photograph whether the seed separates from the stem. Ask about seed origin and disinfection: hot-water treatment at 60 °C for 10 minutes and salt-water selection at specific gravity 1.13 are the practices cited in NCPMS. Ask about nursery temperature, upland versus flooded seedbeds, protected nursery production, and dense sowing. [Source 1](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000752) [Source 2](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bakanae) [Source 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5675463/)
*Features requiring laboratory tests:* Stunting type/asymptomatic infection determination, pathogen isolation and morphology (macroconidia 3~5 septum 36~66 × 3~3.5 µm, microconidia in chains 5~12 × 2~3 µm) ([NCPMS bakanae disease](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000752), pathogen characteristics), TEF1α·RPB2 nucleotide sequence species identification, PKS51/NRPS31 marker Pathotype differentiation ([Niehaus et al. 2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5675463/), Methods). The standard domestic seed testing protocol is unverified.
f6_conditions: NCPMS reports optimum disease development at a nursery temperature of 35 °C after sowing, disease at about 25 °C, and no symptoms at 20 °C. Fungal growth is optimal at 27–30 °C and sporulation at 24–32 °C; spores disperse at night or in light rain. The aerobic pathogen spreads more readily in upland seedbeds and protected nurseries than flooded seedbeds, and dense sowing increases disease. Secondary infection through main-field soil was not reported in that account. Infected seed is the main source, and contaminated soaking water also spreads the pathogen (IRRI). Quantitative evidence for nitrogen effects was not verified. [Source 1](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000752) [Source 2](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bakanae)

f1_names: NCPMS is registered as **false smut**(稻麴病, False smut), pathogen *Ustilaginoidea virens* (Cooke) Takahashi ([NCPMS false smut](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000814), basic information; [Nongsaro mirror](https://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/pss/pssa/sicknsSearchDtl.ps?pageIndex=1&pageSize=10&sicknsCode=D00000814&menuId=PS00202)). LPDK is also the same name/scientific name and does not have a synonym ([LPDK Search](https://genebank.rda.go.kr/plntDissInfoMain.do)). EPPO(USTNVI) synonym is *Claviceps virens*, *Ustilaginoidea oryzae*, *Ustilago virens*, *Villosiclava virens*, English name is false smut, green smut of rice ([EPPO USTNVI](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/USTNVI), Overview). The sexual morph *Villosiclava virens* was proposed by Tanaka et al. (Mycotaxon 106:491–501) (search summary) ([PestInfo wiki](https://wiki.pestinfo.org/wiki/Mycotaxon_(2009)_106,_491-501)). Current classification (Index Fungorum/MycoBank) is unverified.
f2_parts_stages: Visible disease affects rice grains. The pathogen overwinters as sclerotia and chlamydospores. NCPMS describes sclerotial germination in July–August, ascospore deposition on leaf sheaths at booting, and invasion of rice flowers at flowering. Symptoms become visible only after panicle emergence (IRRI). [Source 1](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000814) [Source 2](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/false-smut)
f3_symptoms: The rice grain surface turns yellow-green, the husk opens, yellow-green extrusions form, and then turn black into powder-like chlamydospores. The inside is white, and the outside is dark green to black ([NCPMS false smut](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000814), symptom description). IRRI writes that velvety spore masses (early orange → yellow-green, black-green), immature spore masses wrapped in a membrane, only some grains in the ear are infected, and surrounding grains tend to become unfilled grains ([IRRI RKB False smut](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/false-smut), How to identify).
f4_confusions: A similar disease registered domestically is rice kernel smut (Kernel smut, *Tilletia barclayana*), but the authoritative source that lists the criteria for distinguishing between the two diseases is unverified ([LPDK search](https://genebank.rda.go.kr/plntDissInfoMain.do)).) and the same heading stage ear disease (panicle blast, bacterial grain rot) and the same period overlap ([Rural Development Administration press release 2024-08-01](https://www.rda.go.kr/board/board.do?mode=view&prgId=day_farmprmninfoEntry&dataNo=100000797460), introduction paragraph). The source of the abiotic disturbance comparison is unverified.
f5_differentiation:
*Features assessable in photographs:* Round spore masses formed instead of grains, color change from yellow-green to black-green, surface powder, only some grains within one ear are affected. NCPMS writes that it is "easily identified because it forms conspicuous smut balls on the panicles" ([NCPMS false smut](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000814), Symptom description; [IRRI RKB False smut](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/false-smut)).) Among 26 diseases, the reliability of discrimination based on photos alone is high, but the criteria for distinguishing between the early stage and kernel smut have not been confirmed.
*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* Cross-sectional photo of the spore mass (white inside, greenish black outside). heading stage Number of rainy days and sunshine before and after, nitrogen (especially late fertilization), overuse of organic fertilizers, use of silicate fertilizers, use of rice seeds in disease-affected fields ([NCPMS false smut](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000814), occurrence environment and control methods).
*Features requiring laboratory tests:* Microscopic examination of spores when the distinction from kernel smut, etc. is unclear (the source specifying this is unverified, inferred).
f6_conditions: Domestic: It occurs frequently when there is high humidity due to frequent rain before and after panicle grain set, **temperature is low around 25℃**, little sunlight, and nitrogen is excessive ([Rural Development Administration Press Release 2024-08-01](https://www.rda.go.kr/board/board.do?mode=view&prgId=day_farmprmninfoEntry&dataNo=100000797460)). NCPMS states that low temperature and high humidity, lack of sunlight, and number of rainy days have an “absolute influence”, and nitrogen late-fertilization is encouraged, and silicate fertilizers are Write down that it is suppressed ([NCPMS false smut](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000814), occurrence environment/control method). IRRI: **RH over 90%, 25-35 ℃**, rain/high humidity/high nitrogen soil ([IRRI RKB False smut](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/false-smut)).) The two expressions ("when low to around 25 ℃" vs. "25-35 ℃") are different, so a combination is required. The damage is a decrease in the weight of a thousand grains, a decrease in germination rate of up to 35%, a 25% loss in high humidity, and 7-75% in India (same IRRI page).

user_name: Bacterial panicle blight / bacterial grain rot
section_title: Bacterial panicle blight / bacterial grain rot — *Burkholderia glumae*
f1_names: NCPMS refers to **bacterial grain rot**(枯細菌病, Bacterial grain rot), pathogen *Burkholderia glumae* (Kurita & Tabei) Urakami et al. Registered as [= *Pseudomonas glumae*] ([NCPMS bacterial grain rot](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000742), basic information·pathogen information). LPDK lists *B. glumae* and ***B. plantarii*** together under "bacterial grain rot / bacterial sheath rot" (DSNM_NO 1418), and ***B. gladioli* is listed separately** under "stem blight" (Sheath rot) ([LPDK search](https://genebank.rda.go.kr/plntDissInfoMain.do), host rice bacteria result table). EPPO (PSDMGM)'s English name is bacterial grain rot, colored rice, ear blight, seedling blight of rice ([EPPO PSDMGM](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/PSDMGM)).) It is called "bacterial grain rot" in Asia and "bacterial panicle blight" in the United States and Central and South America. The rice pathogen was transferred to the genus *Burkholderia* in 1994 ([Ham et al. 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6640401/), Introduction). The press release and the 2001 paper use a variation of the term “bacterial rice grain blight.”
f2_parts_stages: It is mainly rice grain, and there are symptoms in the leaf sheath as well. Infected seeds are unable to germinate and rot, and the seedlings die after browning of the leaf sheath ([NCPMS bacterial grain rot](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000742), symptom description). It overwinters in seeds, spreads to healthy seeds during soaking, and lurks in leaf sheaths before invading rice grains at the heading stage (same page, occurrence environment). The heading and flowering periods are the most vulnerable ([Ham et al. 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6640401/), Symptoms). A 2015 Rural Development Administration report stated that "symptoms appear only on rice grains," which is different from NCPMS ("symptoms even on leaf sheaths") ([Rural Development Administration press release 2015-07-29](https://korea.kr/news/pressReleaseView.do?newsId=156066598)).
f3_symptoms: Grains discolor from the base, becoming yellowish white as discoloration spreads. Early-infected panicles become pale reddish, remain upright rather than bending, and contain unfilled grains. Brown rice from late-infected grains is small and has brown streaks (NCPMS). The Arkansas description notes white to light-gray discoloration of the lower third of the glume, separated by a reddish-brown boundary; the panicle axis initially remains green, and dark-brown lesions may occur on the flag-leaf sheath. [Source 1](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000742) [Source 2](https://www.uaex.uada.edu/publications/pdf/FSA-7580.pdf)
f4_confusions: *B. gladioli*·*B. plantarii* cause the same group of symptoms and are distinguished by gyrB multiplex PCR ([Ham et al. 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6640401/)). *Acidovorax avenae* (with grain discoloration) and *Pseudomonas fuscovaginae* also cause grain discoloration (same paper). It can be confused with pest damage such as wind damage, water stress (partial infertility), and striped rice stem borer ([FSA7580](https://www.uaex.uada.edu/publications/pdf/FSA-7580.pdf), Disease Symptoms last paragraph·Fig. 8–9). Domestic "head blight" (*Alternaria*, *Curvularia lunata*, *Fusarium* spp. ([LPDK Search](https://genebank.rda.go.kr/plntDissInfoMain.do)).) Official data directly comparing high temperature infertility is unverified.
f5_differentiation:
*Features assessable in photographs:* For preliminary suspicion: yellowish-white to brown discoloration beginning at the grain base, a reddish-brown boundary, upright panicles, a green panicle axis, flag-leaf-sheath lesions, and patches within the field. Photographs cannot distinguish the causal bacterial species or confirm the diagnosis. [Source 1](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000742) [Source 2](https://www.uaex.uada.edu/publications/pdf/FSA-7580.pdf) [Source 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6640401/)
*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* Ask about maximum and night temperatures around heading and flowering, rainfall and duration of dew, seed disinfection (salt-water selection at specific gravity 1.13–1.14, hot water at 55 °C for 60 minutes, dry heat at 40 °C for 2 days, as cited in NCPMS), pregermination and nursery temperatures (avoiding 30–35 °C), nitrogen application, and seeding rate. [Source 1](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000742) [Source 2](https://www.uaex.uada.edu/publications/pdf/FSA-7580.pdf) [Source 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6640401/)
*Features requiring laboratory tests:* Colonies on S-PG selective medium, toxoflavin pigment on King's B medium (yellow for Ham 2011, "light green" for NCPMS), lipase-pectinase reaction, 16S–23S rDNA spacer primer, seed quantitative real-time PCR, gyrB multiplex, rep-PCR, tobacco leaf hypersensitivity reaction ([Ham et al. 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6640401/), Detection; [NCPMS bacterial grain rot](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000742), pathogen characteristic). The pathogen is a gram-negative short rod-shaped bacterium 0.7 × 1.5~2.5 µm, 1–3 polar flagella, optimal temperature 30~35℃.
f6_conditions: Domestic: Large outbreaks occur during high temperatures and humidity during the planting and flowering periods. Easily occur when pathogenic bacteria are over 10² CFU/mL and temperatures are over 20 ℃. There is no difference in resistance between domestic varieties ([NCPMS bacterial grain rot](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000742), occurrence environment); ** High temperatures over 30 ℃ before and after planting, or frequent rain around 30 mm** ([Rural Development Administration press release) 2015-07-29](https://korea.kr/news/pressReleaseView.do?newsId=156066598)). In the analysis of 1992~2000, the high occurrence years (1994, 1995, 1998, 2000) overlapped with high temperatures and continuous rainfall in the heading stage (early to mid-August) for mid-late-growing species, 1993 had a lot of rain but low temperatures, and 1997 had high temperatures but little rain. There was little occurrence. heading stage When treated in a wet room for more than 24 hours after inoculation, the disease occurred at 10² CFU/mL ([Plant Disease Research 7(3):150-154, 2001](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO200111921139724.page?lang=ko), Abstract). Overseas: Growth temperature is 11~40℃, optimal temperature is 30~35℃, especially large outbreaks occur at **high temperatures at night** ([Ham et al. 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6640401/), Epidemiology); In the United States, high summer night temperatures, long dews, high nitrogen, and excessive sowing promote it ([FSA7580](https://www.uaex.uada.edu/publications/pdf/FSA-7580.pdf), Favorable Conditions).
f7_occurrence: Korea: The earliest LPDK literature is Naejeongba et al. 1987 (Japanese Medicine Research Institute 53(3):402) and Jae-eul Choi 1988, and it is unverified whether this is the first report in Korea ([LPDK Search](https://genebank.rda.go.kr/plntDissInfoMain.do)). Year of occurrence is 1994, 1995, 1998, and 2000 (see [Plant Disease Research 2001](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO200111921139724.page?lang=ko)).). Strain BGR1 is a Korean diseased ear isolate ([Ham et al. 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6640401/)). *B. plantarii* The first report in Korea was Ra et al. It is 2016 ([Search LPDK](https://genebank.rda.go.kr/plntDissInfoMain.do); [SIPaV](https://sipav.org/en/16/Archive/3767),) check only the titles). Overseas: First reported in Japan in 1956, then East Asia, China, Central and South America, and the United States (Louisiana 1995, 1998, 2000 outbreak, up to 75% loss) ([Ham et al. 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6640401/)); Arkansas losses in 1995·2010·2011([FSA7580](https://www.uaex.uada.edu/publications/pdf/FSA-7580.pdf), About the Disease). The EPPO distribution page is 404.
f8_quarantine: Korea: ***B. glumae* is not listed(confirmed)**. The list of bacteria in Annex Table 2 of the Notice includes *B. caryophylli* and ***B. plantarii*** ([KR-Notice Annex 2](https://www.law.go.kr/LSW/flDownload.do?flSeq=169519059)). *B. plantarii* are registered in the LPDK as a domestic outbreak in 2016, but remain as regulated quarantine pests. According to the definition of the law, quarantine pests include "distributed in some areas of the country, but outbreak prevention, etc. It is not necessarily contradictory as it also includes “pests for which measures are being taken” ([Plant Quarantine Act](https://www.law.go.kr/법령/식물방역법), Article 2, Paragraph 5). EPPO: A1/A2 not listed, country entry is Egypt A1, Argentina A1, Brazil A1, Mexico QP, China QP(2021)([EPPO PSDMGM](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/PSDMGM/categorization)). EU: not listed(check)([EU-2072](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:02019R2072-20261015)). United States: not select agent([US-331](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-7/section-331.3)). China: **检疫性有害生物** "水疫细菌性谷枯病菌"([CN](https://assets.ippc.int/static/media/files/reportingobligation/2025/01/07/CATALOGUE_OF_QUARANTINE_PESTS_FOR_IMPORT_PLANTS_TO_THE_PEOPLES_REPUBLIC_OF_CHINA_updated_20241128.doc)). Japan: not listed(verified)([JP](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/325M50010000073)). Australia: unverified.

section_title: Rice stripe — Rice stripe virus(*Tenuivirus oryzaclavatae*)
f1_names: If you search for "stripes" in the NCPMS disease name search, **"rice stripe (Stripe, virus)"** appears as the paddy rice item ([NCPMS disease list](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoListRM.np), Korean name/English name search result table). However, the detailed page and the original text of the List of Plant Diseases in Korea are unverified because they cannot be accessed. Domestic academic journals use “ricerice stripe” and the virus name “rice stripe leaf blight virus (RSV)” ([Lee et al. 2012, Plant Disease Research 18(4):402–405](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO201205759624605.pdf), title, 1 paragraph; [Jeong Bong-jo 1974](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO197425720625117.pub), title). The ICTV 2024 synonymous species name is ***Tenuivirus oryzaclavatae*** (Phenuiviridae, *Tenuivirus*; synonym Rice stripe tenuivirus), and Wikipedia cites ICTV MSL #40 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rice_stripe_virus), classification box; ICTV original text unopened) and EPPO also uses the same name (RSV000) ([EPPO RSV000](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/RSV000/distribution)).
f2_parts_stages: Leaves develop stripes, and panicles may be malformed, sterile, or fail to emerge fully. Seedlings through early tillering are most susceptible; infection after maximum tillering produces milder symptoms (Lucid/IRRI). Incubation is 7–15 days after inoculation at the 3–7-leaf stage and 15–30 days after inoculation at the 9–15-leaf stage (Jeong 1974). [Source 1](https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/key-server/data/0e090d01-0209-460e-810c-0d060708030c/media/Html/Stripe_(Rice_stripe_virus) [Source 2](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO197425720625117.pub)
f3_symptoms: Leaves develop yellowish-white stripes, mottling, and necrotic streaks. Infected seedlings have folded, twisted, wilted, drooping leaves; plants are stunted, with fewer tillers and panicles, and white to brown malformed panicles (Lucid). Wang et al. 2022 instead describe slight stunting with normal tiller numbers. The drooping seedlings that dry out and die gave rise to the Japanese name Yurei Byo (ghost disease), according to the source cited in the original research. [Source 1](https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/key-server/data/0e090d01-0209-460e-810c-0d060708030c/media/Html/Stripe_(Rice_stripe_virus) [Source 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9609659/) [Source 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rice_stripe_virus)
f4_confusions: Domestic researchers state that **"RSV symptoms are very difficult to distinguish from physiological disorders with the naked eye"** ([Lee et al. 2004, Plant Disease Research 10(1):30–33](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO200411922293908.page), abstract). Zinc deficiency shows dusty brown spots on the upper leaves and mid-green yellowing at the base of young leaves 2 to 4 weeks after transplanting ([Lucid Factsheet "Zinc deficiency"](https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/key-server/data/0e090d01-0209-460e-810c-0d060708030c/media/Html/Zinc_deficiency.htm); This page does not directly compare RSV). Black-striped rice dwarf (RBSDV, also vectored by the small brown planthopper) has increased tillering, dark green leaves, and white to black waxy nodules on the leaf veins on the underside of the leaves. Grassy stunt (RGSV) has greatly increased tillering and leaves are short, straight, and light green to light yellow. Rice dwarf (RDV) has dark green leaves with fine yellow-white spots and increased tillering, and its insect vector is the green rice leafhopper ([Wang et al. 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9609659/), Table 2·3).
f5_differentiation:
*Features assessable in photographs:* Yellow-white stripes and necrotic streaks on new leaves, drooping or twisted seedlings (ghost-like appearance), normal or reduced tillering, non-emergence of ears, or deformities ([Lucid Factsheet "Stripe"](https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/key-server/data/0e090d01-0209-460e-810c-0d060708030c/media/Html/Stripe_(Rice_stripe_virus).htm); [Wang et al. 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9609659/)). There is a domestic statement that it is difficult to distinguish from physiological disorders, so photos are used only for the first screening.
*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* Close-up photos of the entire plant and new leaves, photos of rows near the rice paddy bank (more on the side of the rice paddy bank, decreasing towards the center) ([Jeong Bong-jo 1974](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO197425720625117.pub)), presence or absence of small brown planthopper, early transplantation/direct sowing, early-growing susceptible varieties (Woonkwang rice, Odae rice, Ilpoom rice, etc.) ([Lee et al. 2012](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO201205759624605.pdf)), Insecticide treatment of the seedbed and whether it is adjacent to a barley field ([Seung-oh Yoo 2008](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO200856450901109.pdf)), Whether it is on the west coast and when it flies.
*Features requiring laboratory tests:* RT-PCR detected approximately 1,023-bp RdRp and 969-bp CP products from diseased plants and small brown planthoppers (Lee et al. 2004, abstract). A 2012 nationwide survey tested 82 samples by RT-PCR using a 700-bp product (Lee et al. 2012, Fig. 2). An ELISA assay for virus-carrying small brown planthoppers was mentioned in a Gyeonggi agricultural research report, available only as a search snippet. Sap inoculation is unsuitable because the virus is poorly transmitted through sap, according to the cited account. [Source 1](https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/key-server/data/0e090d01-0209-460e-810c-0d060708030c/media/Html/Stripe_(Rice_stripe_virus) [Source 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9609659/) [Source 3](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO197425720625117.pub) [Source 4](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO201205759624605.pdf) [Source 5](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO200856450901109.pdf) [Source 6](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO200411922293908.page) [Source 7](https://nongup.gg.go.kr/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2013/08/20030074.pdf) [Source 8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rice_stripe_virus)
f6_conditions: The cited Korean study gives an optimum transmission temperature of 25–30 °C, rare or absent transmission at 15 °C or below, and five annual generations of the small brown planthopper in Korea. About 90% of offspring of two virus-carrying parents carry the virus through transovarial transmission; acquisition by nonviruliferous insects is about 7–9%, with third- to fifth-instar nymphs most efficient. Of 35 crop, pasture, and weed species tested, 21 were susceptible (Jeong 1974). A laboratory colony had a 52–63% virus-carrier rate, which is not a field estimate (Yi et al. 2015). The vector latent/circulation period is 5–21 days (Wang et al. 2022). Proposed contributors to the 2007 epidemic were untreated seedbeds, early-transplanted and direct-seeded rice providing food for overwintered viruliferous insects, warmer winters (Seocheon +0.8 °C; Buan +2.0 °C), and increased susceptible varieties (Yoo 2008). The first west-coast migration in 2012 was on May 28, concentrated in Jeonbuk and Chungnam, with counts of 1–302 insects (Lee et al. 2012). Risk is greatest when viruliferous planthoppers move from cereal crops to rice. [Source 1](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO197425720625117.pub) [Source 2](https://koreascience.kr/article/JAKO201510659891088.do) [Source 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9609659/) [Source 4](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO200856450901109.pdf) [Source 5](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO201205759624605.pdf) [Source 6](https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/key-server/data/0e090d01-0209-460e-810c-0d060708030c/media/Html/Stripe_(Rice_stripe_virus)
f7_occurrence: Korea: National average incidence rate was about 6.5% in 1965, decreased by resistant cultivars (Nakdong rice) and pest control in the 1980s, **about 4,663 ha in Ganghwa in 2001, 14,137 ha nationwide in 2007, 21,541 ha on the west coast in 2009**, 525 ha in 2010, 7,397 ha in 2011; In the 2012 national survey, the incidence rate decreased from 19.9% in 2008 to 4.9% ([Lee et al. 2012](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO201205759624605.pdf), Text·Table 2·Fig. 3). In 2007, Seocheon occurred in 2,610 ha, or 25% of the total area ([Yoo Seung-oh 2008](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO200856450901109.pdf)). Wikipedia's "84% damage to Korean rice fields in 2007–08" conflicts with domestic primary data (2008 outbreak area rate 19.9%), so domestic data is used) takes precedence ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rice_stripe_virus), Distribution). The area of occurrence by year since 2013 is unverified. Overseas: EPPO (updated 2020-06-23) lists China (restricted), Japan, North Korea, **South Korea "Present, no details"**, Taiwan, Vietnam, and the Russian Far East and South ([EPPO RSV000 distribution](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/RSV000/distribution)). First reported in Japan in 1897, 30-40% supervised in eastern China in 2002-2004 ([Wang et al. 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9609659/), Section 2.1).
f8_quarantine: Korea: **not listed(check)**. "Rice stripe necrosis virus (= *Benyvirus oryzae*)" in Schedule 2 of the Notice is a different virus ([KR-Notice Schedule 2](https://www.law.go.kr/LSW/flDownload.do?flSeq=169519059)). EPPO: A1/A2 not listed, country items include Mexico QP (2018), **US QP (1989)**([EPPO RSV000](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/RSV000/categorization)). EU, China, Japan: not listed (confirmed)([EU-2072](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:02019R2072-20261015); [CN](https://assets.ippc.int/static/media/files/reportingobligation/2025/01/07/CATALOGUE_OF_QUARANTINE_PESTS_FOR_IMPORT_PLANTS_TO_THE_PEOPLES_REPUBLIC_OF_CHINA_updated_20241128.doc); [JP](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/325M50010000073)). United States: QP (1989) according to EPPO tally or official text unverified; insect vector *Laodelphax striatellus* is APHIS Pests of Concern No. 46 (the virus itself is not)([US-PoC](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/laws-regs/animal-plant-diseases-pests-concern)). Australia: unverified. The "Quarantine information unverified" in the rice group 3 note was resolved by this text collation.

section_title: Rice dwarf — Rice dwarf virus(*Phytoreovirus alphaoryzae*)
f1_names: The official notation for NCPMS/Plant Disease Name List is **unverified**. Domestic academic journals use “rice dwarf” ([Lee Ki-woon 1986, Journal of the Korean Society of Plant Pathology 2(1):17–21](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO198630710156433.page), title), and in the Gimhae City Preservation Survey, there are separate “rice dwarf” and “black line rice dwarf” (search snippet) ([Gimhae City Agricultural Technology Center](https://www.gimhae.go.kr/01547/01952/02047.web)). ICTV 2024 The species name is ***Phytoreovirus alphaoryzae*** (Sedoreoviridae, *Phytoreovirus*) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rice_dwarf_virus), classification box; ICTV original text not shown), EPPO preferred name is the same (RDV000), synonym is Rice dwarf phytoreovirus, common names are rice dwarf, rice mosaic, rice stunt (search snippet) ([EPPO RDV000](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/RDV000)). ICTV Report considers RDV as an exemplar of *Phytoreovirus* ([ICTV Report](https://ictv.global/report/chapter/sedoreoviridae/sedoreoviridae/phytoreovirus)).
f2_parts_stages: It invades leaves (white spots and streaks) and the entire plant (atrophy, excessive tillering, poor fruiting), and is the only plant reovirus not limited to the phloem ([ICTV Report](https://ictv.global/report/chapter/sedoreoviridae/sedoreoviridae/phytoreovirus), RDV symptoms). Susceptibility values for each growth stage are unverified.
f3_symptoms: White spots and streaks on leaves, stunting, excessive tillering, and failure of panicles to set grain are reported; galls are not formed (ICTV Report). Leaves are short and dark green, with fine chlorotic specks (Wang et al. 2022, Table 2). [Source 1](https://ictv.global/report/chapter/sedoreoviridae/sedoreoviridae/phytoreovirus) [Source 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9609659/)
f4_confusions: RGDV causes reduced tillering and small nodules appear on the veins on the back of leaves. Black-striped rice dwarf (RBSDV) has twisted leaf tips, torn leaf margins, and waxy nodules on the undersides of leaves, and is vectored by the small brown planthopper. Ragged stunt (RRSV) has dark green torn leaves and vein knots, and grassy stunt (RGSV) has light green/light yellow short, straight leaves ([Wang et al. 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9609659/), Table 2·3; [ICTV Report](https://ictv.global/report/chapter/sedoreoviridae/sedoreoviridae/phytoreovirus)). rice dwarf (*Sclerophthora macrospora*, oomycete) shows leaf yellowing spots, shortened leaves, non-sprouting and deformed ears ([Lee et al. 2003, Plant Disease Research 9(1):52–56](https://online-rpd.org/journal/view.php?number=895), abstract). Zinc deficiency also causes atrophy, but reduces tillering ([Lucid Factsheet "Zinc deficiency"](https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/key-server/data/0e090d01-0209-460e-810c-0d060708030c/media/Html/Zinc_deficiency.htm)). Primary data directly comparing RDV and nutritional deficiency are unverified).
f5_differentiation:
*Features assessable in photographs:* Assess stunting, increased tiller number, dark-green leaves, fine white specks or white streaks along leaf veins, and absence of galls. Close-up images of leaf undersides are needed to help distinguish RBSDV and RGDV, which form enations or galls (ICTV Report; Wang et al. 2022). [Source 1](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO198630710156433.page) [Source 2](https://koreascience.kr/article/JAKO197730710440490.do) [Source 3](https://ictv.global/report/chapter/sedoreoviridae/sedoreoviridae/phytoreovirus)
*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* Presence and density of green rice leafhopper, presence or absence of stumps and ratoon rice, and panicle grain set (based on [Lee Ki-woon 1986](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO198630710156433.page) ratoon rice infection data).
*Features requiring laboratory tests:* Antiserum test (RDV purification and antiserum production in Korea in 1977, can be used to detect plants and insect vectors; search snippet) ([Lee Soon-hyung et al. 1977](https://koreascience.kr/article/JAKO197730710440490.do)). As there is no sap transmission and seed transmission, an insect vector inoculation test is required ([ICTV Report](https://ictv.global/report/chapter/sedoreoviridae/sedoreoviridae/phytoreovirus), Transmission)). The source of the domestic RT-PCR protocol is unverified.
f6_conditions: The principal vector is *Nephotettix cincticeps*; *N. nigropictus* and *Recilia dorsalis* also transmit the virus. Transmission is propagative, including transovarial transmission involving the symbiont *Candidatus* Sulcia muelleri (ICTV). The vector latent/circulation period is 12–25 days (Wang et al. 2022). Korean studies report five annual vector peaks and three disease peaks, with overwintered adults and second- and third-generation nymphs as major sources. At the distribution boundary in Uljin, viruliferous nymphs could not overwinter in the field. Feeding initially virus-free nymphs on infected ratoon rice for 11–30 days produced 13.0–18.2% overwintering virus carriers. Ratoon clump infection in a regularly affected Miryang area was 22.4–26.8% (Lee 1986). Temperature and humidity thresholds for transmission and disease were not verified. [Source 1](https://ictv.global/report/chapter/sedoreoviridae/sedoreoviridae/phytoreovirus) [Source 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9609659/) [Source 3](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO198630710156433.page)
f7_occurrence: Korea: EPPO lists Korea as "Present, no details" (distribution updated on 2010-03-04) ([EPPO RDV000 distribution](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/RDV000/distribution)), In the 1986 literature, Miryang's habitual occurrence area and Uljin's marginal area appear ([Lee Ki-un 1986](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO198630710156433.page)).) Domestic outbreak statistics since 2000 It is unverified. Overseas: First recorded in Japan in 1883, with multiple occurrences in southern and central Japan (1889–1979) and Zhejiang Province, China (1969–1973) ([Wang et al. 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9609659/), Section 2.1). EPPO is internally conflicting as Japan, North Korea, and South Korea are marked as present, while China is marked as "Absent, unreliable record" at the national level, while provincial units such as Fujian, Guangdong, and Zhejiang are marked as present ([EPPO RDV000 distribution](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/RDV000/distribution)).

official_kr_name: Unverified in the disease-name database; udbatta disease is named in Korean legislation
f1_names: The Korean disease name was not confirmed anywhere in the List of Plant Diseases in Korea·NCPMS·EPPO (unverified; no Korean search results) ([EPPO BALAOS](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/BALAOS), Overview). However, **In Paragraph 1 of Annex 1 of the Enforcement Rules of the Plant Quarantine Act, the prohibited quarantine pest name is written as "udbatta disease [*Balansia oryzae-sativae*]"** ([KR-Rules Annex 1](https://www.law.go.kr/LSW/flDownload.do?gubun=&flSeq=163692257&bylClsCd=110201)).) Therefore, the name in the law is confirmed, and the name in the disease name list is unverified. The EPPO preferred name is *Balansia oryzae-sativae* Hashioka (BALAOS), the synonym is *Balansia oryzae*, *Ephelis oryzae* Sydow, and the English name is black choke of rice, false ergot, incense rod, udbatta disease ([EPPO BALAOS](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/BALAOS)). There is a classification dispute. The ITS phylogenetic analysis of 33 *Ephelis* isolates from Japan, Korea, China, Nepal, and India pointed out that there was no basis for dividing *E. oryzae* and *E. japonica* and suggested ***E. japonica*** according to naming priority, and that *Balansia oryzae* was not validly published ([Tanaka et al. 2001](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/mycological-research/article/phylogenetic-studies-of-ephelis-species-from-various-locations-and-hosts-in-asia/620F727E95233FBD11FC91864980E3C2), Abstract). Japanese literature also equates *E. oryzae* (= *B. oryzae-sativae*) and adopts *E. japonica* ([Tsukiboshi et al. 2008, JARQ 42(3)](https://www.jircas.go.jp/sites/default/files/publication/jarq/42-03-06_0.pdf), Discussion).
f2_parts_stages: Affects panicles at heading and flag leaves, where white fungal streaks develop along veins before heading. Maximum tillering to panicle initiation favors disease, and seed infection begins at heading (TNAU). Systemic infection usually affects every tiller on a plant; this statement was available only as a search snippet in the original research. [Source 1](https://agritech.tnau.ac.in/expert_system/paddy/cpdisudbtta.html) [Source 2](https://celkau.in/crops/cereals/rice/udbatta.php)
f3_symptoms: A white mycelial mat binds the panicle branches into an erect, dirty-colored cylindrical rod resembling an incense stick, with no grain formation. Before heading, narrow white lines of mycelium and conidia occur along flag-leaf veins (TNAU). Japanese literature describes sterile panicles encased in gray to black stromata, giving a mummified appearance (Tsukiboshi et al. 2008, p.173). [Source 1](https://agritech.tnau.ac.in/expert_system/paddy/cpdisudbtta.html) [Source 2](https://www.jircas.go.jp/sites/default/files/publication/jarq/42-03-06_0.pdf)
f4_confusions: The primary source on the differentiation between this disease and others is **unverified**. Comparisons with commonly thought candidates such as false smut, panicle blast, damage from whitehead-type pests, and non-emergence of rice stem nematodes are not described as there is no basis.
f5_differentiation:
*Features assessable in photographs:* At heading, the entire panicle forms a single rod-like structure with a white to gray-black stromatal coating. Look for white streaks along flag-leaf veins and involvement of all tillers on an affected plant (TNAU; Tsukiboshi et al. 2008). [Source 1](https://agritech.tnau.ac.in/expert_system/paddy/cpdisudbtta.html) [Source 2](https://www.jircas.go.jp/sites/default/files/publication/jarq/42-03-06_0.pdf) [Source 3](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/mycological-research/article/phylogenetic-studies-of-ephelis-species-from-various-locations-and-hosts-in-asia/620F727E95233FBD11FC91864980E3C2)
*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* Whether nearby grasses and weeds (alternative hosts such as *Isachne elegans*, *Cynodon dactylon*, *Pennisetum* sp., *Eragrostis tenuifolia*) have the same symptoms, and seed source ([TNAU](https://agritech.tnau.ac.in/expert_system/paddy/cpdisudbtta.html), Mode of spread).
*Features requiring laboratory tests:* Genus determination by *Ephelis* type conidium microscopic examination ([Tsukiboshi et al. 2008](https://www.jircas.go.jp/sites/default/files/publication/jarq/42-03-06_0.pdf), Discussion), ITS sequence analysis ([Tanaka et al. 2001](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/mycological-research/article/phylogenetic-studies-of-ephelis-species-from-various-locations-and-hosts-in-asia/620F727E95233FBD11FC91864980E3C2)). prohibited quarantine pest, therefore, suspected cases must undergo morphological and molecular identification and confirmation by quarantine agencies in parallel.
f6_conditions: Warm temperature, high humidity, maximum tillering stage ~ panicle initiation stage, and less when sowing at the very early or very late stage. Specific temperature and humidity values are not available in the source. It can spread outside and inside the seed and survive in the residue, and hot water soaking (estimated at 50-54°C for 10 minutes; original text "50-540 C" is incorrect) and Captan·Thiram seed treatment are suggested for control ([TNAU](https://agritech.tnau.ac.in/expert_system/paddy/cpdisudbtta.html), Favorable conditions·Mode of spread·Management). The reliability of the TNAU page is limited because the causal pathogen is misspelled as “bacteria.” It mainly occurs in the hot and humid lowlands of Bihar, Odisha, Maharashtra, and Karnataka in India (search snippet)([krishikosh](https://krishikosh.egranth.ac.in/items/41efb2d8-68f4-40d3-aca9-889e026e1db2/full)).
f7_occurrence: Korea: **Domestic occurrence record unverified.** There is no EPPO distribution in Korea ([EPPO BALAOS distribution](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/BALAOS/distribution)),) No record of rice occurrence was found in domestic literature or NCPMS. The "Korea" isolate from Tanaka 2001 does not have a host (rice or not) in the abstract, so **cannot be used as evidence for the occurrence of Korean rice**. In Japan, the EPPO is "Absent, invalid record", and Japanese literature has no reports of the occurrence of rice at all, and states that it first occurred only in the Japanese family, such as silver grass and sparrow, in 1904 ([Tsukiboshi et al. 2008](https://www.jircas.go.jp/sites/default/files/publication/jarq/42-03-06_0.pdf), p.174). Overseas (EPPO): Sierra Leone, USA (Louisiana; unreliable in Florida), China (Hong Kong, Yunnan), India (Karnataka, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha), Indonesia, New Caledonia, Vanuatu ([EPPO BALAOS distribution](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/BALAOS/distribution)). known as "Udbatta" in India and "Yi-Zhu-Xiang" in China) It is called ([Tsukiboshi et al. 2008](https://www.jircas.go.jp/sites/default/files/publication/jarq/42-03-06_0.pdf), p.173).
f8_quarantine: Korea: **prohibited quarantine pest** — Enforcement Rule Article 4, Subparagraph 1, Item A → **Appendix 1, Subparagraph 1** (<Amended in 2023. 2. 22.>): prohibited plants “rice, rice husk, rice straw and their processed products (excluding peeled rice)”, prohibited area “all areas of the world (excluding Japan and Taiwan)”, prohibited quarantine pest “udbatta disease [*Balansia oryzae-sativae*]”; According to Note 2, North Korea is not included in the prohibited area ([KR-Rule Annex 1](https://www.law.go.kr/LSW/flDownload.do?gubun=&flSeq=163692257&bylClsCd=110201)). EPPO: A1/A2 not listed, country items include Brazil A1 (2018), Mexico QP (2018), **Republic of Korea QP (2018)**, APPPC A2 (1993) ([EPPO BALAOS](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/BALAOS/categorization)). EU·China: not listed(confirmed)([EU-2072](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:02019R2072-20261015); [CN](https://assets.ippc.int/static/media/files/reportingobligation/2025/01/07/CATALOGUE_OF_QUARANTINE_PESTS_FOR_IMPORT_PLANTS_TO_THE_PEOPLES_REPUBLIC_OF_CHINA_updated_20241128.doc)). USA: not select agent, regulatory table unverified([US-331](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-7/section-331.3)). Japan: **検疫有害動植物 +輸入禁止(別表二 15の項) + 侵入調査(別表八)**, "イネミイラ穂病菌"([JP](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/325M50010000073)). Australia: unverified. The “Korean quarantine designation unverified” in the rice group 3 note was resolved in the original text of the law. Japan excludes "the Korean peninsula and Taiwan" from the rice import ban areas, and Korea excludes "Japan and Taiwan". Although it is interpreted that the two countries treat each other as pest-free areas, this is an interpretation based on the contrast between the provisions of the provisions.
