official_kr_name: Disease name unverified; rice stem nematode is the pest name in Korean legislation
f1_names: “ rice stem nematode ” is confirmed as **prohibited quarantine pest name** ( rice stem nematode [*Ditylenchus angustus*]) in Paragraph 1 of Appendix 1 of the Enforcement Rules ([KR-Rules Appendix 1](https://www.law.go.kr/LSW/flDownload.do?gubun=&flSeq=163692257&bylClsCd=110201)). Korean **disease name** corresponding to ufra and Korean Society of Nematology notation are unverified. EPPO carries *Ditylenchus angustus* (Butler) Filipjev(DITYAN), synonym *Anguillulina angusta*, *Tylenchus angustus*, common names akhet-pet, dak pora, rice stem nematode, ufra disease ([EPPO DITYAN datasheet](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/DITYAN/datasheet)). local names are ufra (India), dak pora (Bangladesh), akhet-pet (Myanmar), yadngo (Thailand), and tiem dot san (Vietnam). After Butler (1913) described it in East Bengal, Goodey (1932) and Filipjev (1936) transferred it to the genus ([USDA CAPS 2016](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Ditylenchus-angustus-datasheet-2016.pdf), Common Names·Pest Description). Subbotin & Ryss (2024) narrowly redefined the scope of *Ditylenchus*, so the genus classification remains fluid ([CDFA 2026](https://blogs.cdfa.ca.gov/Section3162/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Ditylenchus-angustus.pdf), History & Status).
f2_parts_stages: The nematode is an ectoparasite of above-ground tissues, especially young leaves, inflorescences, and young seed, and can be recovered from dried stems. It is absent from internodes below the growing point. Leaf yellowing occurs from seedling to flag-leaf stages; panicle symptoms appear after heading. First symptoms are observed about 2 months after transplanting, and early heading is the best survey stage (USDA CAPS 2016). [Source 1](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Ditylenchus-angustus-datasheet-2016.pdf)
f3_symptoms: During the vegetative growth stage, yellowing and deformity of leaves, **white splash-shaped spots at the base of young leaves**, necrotic brown stains on leaves and leaf sheaths, blackening of upper internodes, twisting of bases of young leaves, swelling of lower nodes and irregular branches appear. After heading, the ears are wrinkled and empty, the ears and branches are twisted, **the ears are trapped in the swollen leaf sheath**, or only a part of them comes out. Dark brown patches appear on the field, and during harvest, healthy plants fall over, but infected plants (empty ears) stand upright ([USDA CAPS 2016](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Ditylenchus-angustus-datasheet-2016.pdf), Symptoms Fig. 2–6; [CDFA 2026](https://blogs.cdfa.ca.gov/Section3162/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Ditylenchus-angustus.pdf), Symptoms).
f4_confusions: The rice leaf nematode (*Aphelenchoides besseyi*, white tip) found in Korea is difficult to distinguish at low magnification because the damage and larval and female forms are similar. *A. besseyi* has an esophageal gland that largely overlaps the front of the intestine and has 3-4 projections at the end of the tail. Males do not have a bursa and have 2-4 rows of oocytes, while *D. angustus* males have a bursa and usually have 1 row of oocytes ([USDA CAPS 2016](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Ditylenchus-angustus-datasheet-2016.pdf), Easily Confused Pests·Pest Description). The primary source for comparison with stem borer pests (whiteheads) is unverified. It has been reported that zinc deficiency in soil and plants is related to ufra susceptibility (Miah et al. 1984), and there is a technology that brown spots on the damaged area may be the site of secondary invasion by *Fusarium*, *Sarocladium oryzae*, etc. ([USDA CAPS 2016](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Ditylenchus-angustus-datasheet-2016.pdf), Biology·Known Vectors).
f5_differentiation:
*Features assessable in photographs:* White splash spots at the base of young leaves, twisted leaf bases and flag leaves, ears trapped in swollen leaf sheaths, black browning between upper internodes, dark brown patches in the field, and empty ears standing upright at harvest time ([USDA CAPS 2016](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Ditylenchus-angustus-datasheet-2016.pdf), Symptoms). Low-density infections are difficult to detect with the naked eye (same document, Survey). The judgment that the absence of borers or larvae in the stem cross section is a clue to distinguishing from pest damage is an inference.
*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* Deep or long-term flooding, irrigation water inflow route, history of imported seeds or plants, presence of stumps or ratoon rice.
*Features requiring laboratory tests:* Extract nematodes by cutting dried leaves and stems into approximately 55-mm pieces, splitting them lengthwise, and soaking them for 24 hours; dissect young inflorescences under water, use a Baermann funnel for 24 hours, or use a mist chamber. Collect tissue above the panicle neck (USDA CAPS 2016). Identification uses tail shape and size, relative lengths of the stylet and post-uterine sac, and four lateral lines; females measure 0.8–1.2 mm, with a 10–11 µm stylet and V=78–80. Esterase/protein profiles and rDNA PCR help distinguish *Aphelenchoides*. As a prohibited quarantine pest in the original research, suspected findings require notification to the quarantine authority. [Source 1](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Ditylenchus-angustus-datasheet-2016.pdf)
f6_conditions: Infection is optimal at 27–30 °C, with a 10–20-day life cycle. Movement on leaves requires RH of at least 75%. Irrigation spreads nematodes; most die within days in water, but they can invade young rice within an hour. This is a major pest of deepwater rice flooded more than 50 cm for over a month, and occurs sporadically in irrigated and rainfed rice. At harvest, nematodes survive by anhydrobiosis inside dry glumes of lower spikelets, primarily as J4 juveniles. At least three generations occur per crop (USDA CAPS). Seed transmission remains disputed: Prasad & Varaprasad 2002 reported it, while Bridge & Starr 2007 and CABI 2021 assessed the risk as small (CDFA). Hosts include *Oryza* spp., *Leersia hexandra*, *Echinochloa colona*, *Sacciolepis interrupta*, and wheat. Reported yield losses are 20–90% in India/Thailand, 50–100% in Vietnam, and 40–60% in Bangladesh. [Source 1](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Ditylenchus-angustus-datasheet-2016.pdf) [Source 2](https://blogs.cdfa.ca.gov/Section3162/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Ditylenchus-angustus.pdf)
f7_occurrence: Korea: **Domestic outbreak records unverified.** Neither North nor South Korea are included in the EPPO distribution table ([EPPO DITYAN distribution](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/DITYAN/distribution)),) No literature on domestic outbreaks was found. The official document specifying “non-occurrence in the country” is unverified, and can only be judged indirectly due to the prohibited quarantine pest designation and the absence of a distribution table. Overseas (EPPO): Bangladesh (widespread), India (Assam and West Bengal), Malaysia (West), Myanmar, Philippines, Thailand, Vietnam (restricted); Madagascar “pest no longer present”; Egypt, Sudan, Indonesia, Pakistan "Absent, unreliable record"([EPPO DITYAN distribution](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/DITYAN/distribution)). USDA CAPS 2016 includes Indonesia as a distribution country, and CDFA 2026 includes Madagascar as a distribution country, which is different from EPPO ([USDA CAPS 2016](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Ditylenchus-angustus-datasheet-2016.pdf); [CDFA 2026](https://blogs.cdfa.ca.gov/Section3162/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Ditylenchus-angustus.pdf)). It has not occurred in the United States and California (CDFA 2026).
